Threat.value: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'explosion or bang sounds' is a poor fit unless there was a firearm discharge or similar blast-like cue; nothing else in the profile suggests that context, so this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'I have lost my connection to my community and culture' is difficult to justify from the rest of this profile for an adult European married teacher after a mugging/robbery. The other appraisals focus on self-blame/institutional failure, but this item implies a broader cultural/community rupture that is not supported by the trauma type, demographics, or other nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, the profile otherwise centers on external danger, sensory reliving, and mistrust/injustice. 'Violated Values' implies the patient did something morally incongruent during the event, but there are no accompanying memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting perpetration, betrayal of others, failure to act, or shame-based self-condemnation. In this profile it stands apart from the rest of the formulation and is the least clinically coherent item.

vignette: Andreas had always loved his job as a high school teacher, but everything changed on that fateful evening three years ago. As he was walking home from a staff meeting, lost in thought about an upcoming lesson plan, two men jumped out of the shadows and mugged him. They grabbed his briefcase and wallet, pushing him to the ground before fleeing into the crowded streets. Andreas remembered the taste of blood in his mouth as he struggled to get up, dazed and disoriented. In the weeks that followed, Andreas began to notice a change within himself. He would find himself scanning the faces of strangers on the street, searching for any sign of threat or hostility. His eyes would dart back and forth, taking in every detail, from the way they carried themselves to the expression on their face. It was as if he had developed a sixth sense, always on high alert for potential danger. He couldn't shake off the feeling that anyone could be a threat, and it made him anxious in crowded places. Driving with his wife, Rachel, became a source of tension. Andreas would tense up whenever she made sudden movements or took her eyes off the road. He knew it wasn't rational, but he just couldn't help it - every unexpected turn or brake felt like a potential attack waiting to happen. Loud noises, especially those that sounded like footsteps or shouting, made him jump out of his skin. Andreas tried to explain to Rachel why these things unsettled him so much, but even he struggled to put into words the fear that gripped him. It was as if his mind had become wired to detect danger everywhere, and it left him feeling perpetually on edge. He began to avoid crowded places altogether, opting for quiet coffee shops or solo walks in the park instead of joining friends for a night out. But no matter how hard he tried, Andreas couldn't escape the memories of that fateful night. The taste of blood would flood back into his mouth without warning, transporting him back to the scene of the crime. It was as if every sense - sight, sound, smell - had been imprinted with the horror of that moment, and it could replay itself at any instant. Andreas couldn't understand why this kept happening to him. Hadn't he done everything right? He reported the mugging to the police, gave them a detailed description of his attackers...but nothing seemed to have come of it. The injustice of it all burned within him - why had no one been brought to account for what they did? As time went on, Andreas's world began to shrink. He stopped taking his usual route to school, opting instead for quieter streets that made him feel safer. His relationships with colleagues and friends began to suffer as he pulled away from social gatherings. Even simple tasks like grocery shopping became daunting challenges. It was Rachel who finally convinced Andreas to seek help. She couldn't bear seeing the man she loved live in constant fear, and she knew that things had reached a breaking point when Andreas broke down in tears one evening, overwhelmed by the memories that haunted him. As Andreas sat in his therapist's office for the first time, he knew that he was taking a crucial step towards reclaiming his life. He wanted to learn how to calm the storm raging within him, to quiet the voices that told him danger lurked around every corner. Most of all, he longed to rediscover the sense of safety and security that had been torn from him on that fateful night. With a deep breath, Andreas began to share his story, hoping against hope that somehow, someway, he could learn to heal and move forward once more.
